newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia'a ruling party galloping to poll victory.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia'a ruling party galloping to poll victory.

text.p: Indonesia's ruling Golkar party was well on the way to a forecast landslide victory in parliamentary elections on Thursday, early returns showed.

Nearly 125 million people were eligible to vote in the national and local elections, which were generally peaceful. Police reported 13 people were killed overnight in the troubled territory of East Timor when rebels tried to disrupt the polls.
A soldier was killed in the territory on Thursday while guarding a poll booth, police added, but no trouble was reported elsewhere in the country.

Figures announced by election officials at 1:30 a.m. Friday (1830 GMT) showed Golkar had taken 78.56 percent, the Moslem-oriented United Development Party (PPP) 18.86 percent and the badly-split Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI) 2.58 percent with over 33.5 million votes counted.

Based on past election patterns of about a 90 percent turnout, the number of votes counted represent about a third of all ballots cast. Election officials said most results would be known by Friday evening.
Golkar won 68 percent of the vote in the last elections in 1992 and had been aiming for just above 70 percent this time round. The PPP won 17 percent of the vote in 1992 and the PDI 15 percent.
Results also showed Golkar well ahead in voting for regional and local assemblies. The three parties are the only ones permitted to contest the elections.

The PPP put on a strong showing during the 27-day election campaign that turned out to be the most violent in three decades. Most of the violence was centred on Java island, which holds 60 percent of the population of 200 million, mainly between partisans of the PPP and Golkar.

Political analysts have expressed concern that PPP supporters might not accept the election outcome if they were swamped in areas where they regarded themselves as strong -- including Jakarta and Central Java.
"It seems to have been very calm and orderly," one senior Asian diplomat said, adding it appeared Golkar could be headed for a landslide in Jakarta.
Markets shrugged off the election in slow trade, with the rupiah stable at 2,441.50 to the dollar and the stock market index jumping two percent on blue chip buying.
In East Timor, police chief Colonel Yusuf Muharam said a soldier guarding a polling booth was shot dead on Thursday, bringing to 14 the number of deaths in the territory since Wednesday night.
He said police had shot dead four rebels in a clash in the centre of Dili on Wednesday night during an attempt to disrupt the elections.
He said rebels shot dead at least seven civilians in the town of Los Palos and two in Baucau in separate attacks on Wednesday as opponents of the government destroyed a number of polling booths.

The rebels are fighting Indonesian rule in East Timor after Jakarta invaded the territory in 1975 and incorporated it as its 27th province the following year. The move has never been recognised by the United Nations.
President Suharto urged people on Wednesday night to exercise their democratic right and duty by voting in an apparent bid to offset dissident calls for a boycott of the polls.
Indonesians voted to elect 425 members to the 500-seat House of Representatives and to regional and local assemblies. The other 75 parliamentary seats are filled by the military which does not vote.
But political analysts say the key election is next March when Suharto, 75, is widely expected to run for a seventh five-year term.
There is keen interest in who he will approve as a running mate, and thus a potential successor.
